claim_assessments.claim_text: Bench-scale batch and isotherm studies with pinewood and date-seed biochars show much stronger sorption (lower equilibrium aqueous concentrations, Ce) for long‑chain PFAS (PFOA, PFOS, PFDA, PFTeDA) than for short‑chain PFHxA and GenX in simple aqueous solutions, even when Ce spans 0–9000 µg/L [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E01 and S03-E08 describe 24 h batch sorption of six PFAS on pinewood and date-seed biochars in aqueous solutions. S03-E04 and E08 report Ce ranges of 0–1000, 2000–4000, and 5000–9000 µg/L and show lower Ce (stronger sorption) for long‑chain PFDA, PFTeDA, PFOS and higher Ce for short‑chain PFHxA and GenX. This matches the chain‑length trend and Ce range described.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Long‑chain compounds give lower Ce on both biochars; PFOS often has the lowest Ce, consistent with high affinity [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E04 explicitly notes that long‑chain PFDA and PFTeDA have low/intermediate Ce and short‑chains have high Ce; it also states that PFOS reported the lowest Ce values, demonstrating great affinity with both biochars. This directly supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Similar chain‑length dependence is seen for modified coal fly ash (CFA‑B): with pure PFAS solutions, the maximum capacity is higher for longer‑chain PFAS than shorter‑chain ones [S11].
claim_assessments.rationale: S11-E03 and S11-E05 state that in pure PFAS solutions CFA achieved 3.5 mg/g capacity and that longer-chain PFAS adsorbed faster and at higher capacities than short‑chain PFAS; S11-E05 also notes Langmuir data showing higher capacity for longer-chain PFAS. This supports the described chain‑length dependence in pure solutions.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Ball‑milled colloidal activated carbon (CAC BM) removes PFOS and PFOA more effectively (89% and 73% removal in 1 h) than PFBS and PFBA (55% and 30%) at 1 mg/L in synthetic water [S07].
claim_assessments.rationale: S07-E06 reports removal efficiencies of 89% (PFOS), 73% (PFOA), 55% (PFBS), and 30% (PFBA). S07-E03 specifies single‑solute batch tests at initial PFAS concentration 1.0 mg/L in aqueous solution for 1 h. Combined, these excerpts support the quantitative claim and conditions.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In multi‑matrix tests, activated carbon and a wood‑derived biochar maintain substantial equilibrium capacities for PFOA, PFOS and GenX (7.7, 16.1, 4.8 mg/g respectively) across Milli‑Q, groundwater and wastewater, despite reduced performance in wastewater [S13].
claim_assessments.rationale: S13-E03 states that AC and BC‑W maintained substantial adsorption capacities of 7.7, 16.1, and 4.8 mg/g for PFOA, PFOS, and GenX respectively across Milli‑Q water, groundwater, and wastewater, and notes decreased performance in wastewater. This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Strong‑base anion exchange resins with quaternary amines generally show higher selectivity for PFSAs over PFCAs and for longer over shorter chains; for example, selectivity ranking across PFAS on AERs was PFOS > PFHxS > PFBS > PFOA > PFHpA > PFHxA > PFPeA > PFBA [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E07 reports selectivity coefficients with overall trend PFOS > PFHxS > PFBS > PFOA > PFHpA > PFHxA > PFPeA > PFBA, and S01-E04 explains higher selectivity for PFSAs and long‑chain PFAS due to acidity and hydrophobicity. This supports both the ordering and the functional‑group/chain‑length statement.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In batch IX with NOM, the resin (quaternary amine, chloride form) shows higher affinity for PFOS than PFOA, consistent with higher charge density and acidity of PFSAs [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E02 reports previous IX capacities higher for PFOS than PFOA on quaternary‑amine resins and explains higher affinity toward PFOS due to resin selectivity; S06-E05 gives PFOS/PFOA charge densities. However, the specific batch NOM experiment comparison PFOS>PFOA is not detailed in the provided chunks, so the mechanistic explanation is supported but the exact experiment context is only indirectly supported.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In mixed PFAS/short-chain PFAA groups, IX outperforms GAC for short‑chain PFAA removal in several waters, attributed primarily to electrostatic attraction between the anionic PFAS and cationic functional groups; this is particularly important for short‑chain compounds with low hydrophobicity [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E02 states that IX was the highest performing short‑chain PFAA adsorbent with lowest use rates, that IX and SMC outperformed GAC for short‑chain PFAAs, and attributes this to electrostatic interactions between anionic PFAAs and cationic functional groups, especially for short‑chain with moderate/low hydrophobicity. This aligns with the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Mixed‐media CPS and ZIPGEM columns treating canal water show adsorption preference PFOS > PFOA > PFHxS > PFHpA > PFHxA > PFPeA > PFBS > PFBA for both media [S09].
claim_assessments.rationale: S09-E01 and S09-E04 report that, in canal water column tests with CPS and ZIPGEM, the general order of adsorption was PFOS > PFOA > PFHxS > PFHpA > PFHxA > PFPeA > PFBS > PFBA. This directly matches the stated preference.

claim_assessments.claim_text: BIPGEM component tests show long‑chain PFAS adsorb strongly to biochar, clay and perlite; short‑chain PFAS and GenX adsorb to biochar and clay but poorly to sand and ZVI, with PFBA exhibiting negative distribution coefficients indicating net desorption tendency [S08].
claim_assessments.rationale: S08-E04 states that high Cs values indicate strong adsorption; Table 4 (described) shows long‑chain PFAS adsorbed well to biochar, clay, and perlite, short‑chain PFAS and GenX adsorbed to biochar and clay but poorly to sand and ZVI. It also notes negative Kd values for PFBA indicating desorption tendency and higher mobility. This supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: IFGEM‑7 shows markedly higher column capacity for PFOS (q0 = 2.59 ng/g) than PFOA (0.007 ng/g), with life‑expectancy calculations predicting orders‑of‑magnitude longer operation for PFOS than PFOA at 100 ng/L influent in a filter scenario [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-R02 quantitative findings list q0 of 2.59 ng/g for PFOS and 0.007 ng/g for PFOA on IFGEM‑7, and estimated life expectancies of 1506 h for PFOS vs 4.2 h for PFOA at 100 ng/L influent and 80% removal. This matches the large disparity in capacity and modeled operation time claimed.

claim_assessments.claim_text: For engineered CAC in simulated groundwater, inorganic anions and DOM suppress adsorption of short‑chain PFAA (<7 perfluorinated carbons) more than long‑chain PFAA (≥7 carbons); short‑chain PFAA therefore show lower retention and shorter modeled barrier lifetimes [S14].
claim_assessments.rationale: S14-E01 reports that inorganic anions decreased adsorption for short‑chain PFAA (<7 carbons) while long‑chain PFAA (≥7 carbons) were less impacted, and that DOM decreased adsorption for all PFAA in a chain‑length dependent manner. S14-E04 and E07 state that groundwater solutes significantly lower retention and barrier performance for short‑chain PFAA, leading to lower lifetimes than for long‑chain PFAA. This supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Long‑chain PFSAs (e.g., PFOS, PFHxS) are consistently the most “adsorbable” species across carbons, IX, and specialty media under the examined conditions.
claim_assessments.rationale: Multiple sources show PFOS (a long‑chain PFSA) having highest adsorption or selectivity: S01-E07 (AER selectivity), S03-E04 (lowest Ce), S04-E05 (later breakthrough than PFBS/PFHxA), S07-E06 (highest removal), S08-E06 (long‑chain stronger removal), S11-E05 (higher capacity for long chains in pure solutions), S13-E05 (PFOS > PFOA > GenX), S15-E01 (only PFOS qe>1 mg/g for biochar). However, PFHxS is not consistently documented as ‘most adsorbable’ across all media in the provided excerpts, and the strong generalization “across carbons, IX, and specialty media” goes beyond any single source. Without explicit cross‑media synthesis in the cited records, this broad summary is only partially supported.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Ether‑based alternatives (e.g., GenX) frequently show lower adsorption selectivity on AERs and carbons than legacy PFOS/PFOA [S01, S03, S07, S09].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E04 notes low adsorption selectivity of AERs for GenX compared to other PFAS, and S13 (not cited here) plus S03-E04 indicate weaker sorption for GenX vs PFOS/PFOA on biochars. However, S07 and S09 excerpts provided do not mention GenX; S07 tests only PFBA, PFBS, PFOA, PFOS, and S09 focuses on PFOS, PFOA and several shorter PFAAs. Thus the statement is supported for some AERs and some carbons but not across all cited sources, and the adverb “frequently” plus inclusion of S07 and S09 is broader than the evidence shown.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Pinewood biochar’s mesoporous structure is associated with stronger uptake (lower Ce) for long‑chain PFAS than date‑seed biochar despite similar long‑chain preference on both [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E06 notes that PW’s mesoporous abundance correlates with lower Ce values for long-chain PFAS (PFOS, PFDA, PFTeDA) compared to DS biochar, implying higher capacity despite similar overall trends. This supports that PW mesoporosity is associated with stronger long‑chain uptake. However, the causal phrasing and the explicit comparison “despite similar long‑chain preference on both” is more interpretive than directly stated, so the mechanistic linkage is partially supported.

claim_assessments.claim_text: ZIPGEM has higher PZC (9.2) than CPS (5.6), yielding positive surface charge over a broader pH range and contributing to stronger PFAS adsorption [S09].
claim_assessments.rationale: S09-E05 reports pH_pzc of ZIPGEM = 9.2 and CPS = 5.6, and explains that these values mean predominantly positive surface charge below those pH values and that ZIPGEM’s higher pH_pzc may be advantageous for PFAS removal in various matrices. This supports the numeric comparison, the broader pH range of positive charge, and implication for stronger adsorption.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Median K_PFAS/Cl ≈ 595 vs K_SO4/Cl ≈ 189 across AER–PFAS combinations [S01], showing PFAS outcompete chloride and often nitrate, but practical competition from sulfate can be significant due to higher sulfate concentrations [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-R02 quantitative findings list median selectivity coefficient ratios K_PFAS/Cl = 595.3 and K_SO4/Cl = 188.9. S01-E07 interprets these as PFAS having highest selectivity relative to chloride and notes that although PFAS vs nitrate and sulfate selectivities are similar, sulfate is more interfering in practice because its concentration is typically higher than nitrate. This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: IFGEM‑7 combines iron‑based components with other media; PFOS capacity (2.59 ng/g) vs much lower PFOA capacity (0.007 ng/g) shows strong functional‑group and hydrophobicity dependence [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-R02 explicitly reports q0 values of 2.59 ng/g (PFOS) and 0.007 ng/g (PFOA) on IFGEM‑7 and describes IFGEM‑7 as an Iron-Filings-based Green Environmental Media mixture, implying iron‑based plus other components. The interpretation that this difference “shows strong functional‑group and hydrophobicity dependence” is qualitatively consistent with PFOS vs PFOA behavior but is not explicitly stated in the source, so mechanism attribution is inferential.

claim_assessments.claim_text: CPS (clay–perlite–sand) and ZIPGEM (adding ZVI) differ in BET surface area, porosity and PZC; ZIPGEM’s higher surface area and PZC support higher removal of some short‑chain PFAS (e.g., PFBS) compared with CPS at 2 h [S09].
claim_assessments.rationale: S09-E05 states that ZIPGEM has higher density, BET surface area, porosity, hydraulic conductivity, and higher pH_pzc than CPS due to ZVI. S09-E01 reports that at 2 h, PFBS removal was ~72% (CPS) vs ~90% (ZIPGEM). Thus the factual difference in performance and properties is supported. The causal statement that higher surface area and PZC “support” higher removal is mechanistic inference, not directly tested in the excerpt, so the mechanistic part is only partially supported.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In tap water at ~5 ng/L, sulfonamide acetic acid precursors (EtFOSAA, MeFOSAA, C8) show higher sorption than PFCAs of similar chain length, attributed to additional electrostatic interactions from combined sulfonamide and carboxylic groups [S12].
claim_assessments.rationale: S12-E08 states that for C8 sulfonamide acetic acids (EtFOSAA and MeFOSAA), the presence of both sulfonamide and carboxylic groups enhanced sorption compared to PFCA of same chain length (C9), attributing this to additional electrostatic interactions. S12-E05 describes the 5 ng/L tap‑water setup. Thus both the comparative sorption and mechanistic attribution are supported.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In batch IX studies with PFOA/PFOS and different NOM isolates at 5 mg C/L, DOC removals >60% were achieved concurrently with complete PFAS removal under some conditions, but humic isolates (higher MW) caused pore blockage and size exclusion, limiting PFAS uptake and reducing model predictiveness [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E04 reports that IX achieved complete PFAS removal with simultaneous >60% DOC removal; S06-E03 and E05 specify NOM isolates at 5 mg C/L and note evidence of size exclusion and pore blockage by humic and higher MW fractions (e.g., SRHA) that limited uptake and affected EBC model applicability. This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In more complex waters (wastewater effluent, membrane concentrate, landfill leachate), IX columns showed rapid breakthrough of short‑chain PFAAs, with >50% C/C₀ reached in <30,000 bed volumes, reflecting strong competition from DOC and inorganic ions [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E02 states that in WW, MC, and LL, removal of short‑chain PFAAs is challenging, with fast breakthrough (>50% C/C0 at <30,000 BV) for IX, and attributes this to DOC and inorganic ions competing for or blocking sites. The numeric breakthrough description is supported. The strength of the causal language (“reflecting strong competition”) is consistent with their interpretation but still somewhat inferential, so partially supported.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In Dutch tap water at 5 ng/L per PFAS, three GACs removed <50% of most PFAS, with only short‑chain precursors showing higher sorption; NOM and low concentration together limit driving force for mass transfer and capacity utilization [S12].
claim_assessments.rationale: S12-E05 reports that tap water spiked with 5 ng/L of each of 31 PFAS treated with three GACs showed removal below 50% for most PFAS, except short‑chain precursors. S12-E02 and E03 discuss that sorption at these realistic low concentrations was relatively low and that hydrophobic/electrostatic interactions plus water chemistry influence sorption, implying limited driving force. While ‘driving force’ language is a paraphrase, the overall statement is consistent with the text.

claim_assessments.claim_text: RSSCTs with eight GACs across four groundwaters show earlier PFBS breakthrough in a higher‑DOC groundwater (Well 4) than in lower‑DOC wells: F400 achieved significant PFBS breakthrough between about 75,000 and >90,000 BVs in lower‑DOC wells, but in Well 4 PFBS 60% breakthrough occurred between ~10,000–20,000 BVs for several GACs [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E06 states that in lower‑DOC Wells 1–3, F400 had significant PFBS breakthrough (BV 60%) at 75,000 to >90,000 BV, whereas in Well 4 (higher DOC) four GACs had PFBS breakthrough at <5000 BV (initial) and 10,000–20,000 BV at BV 60%, and the remaining four at 5000–10,000 BV initial and 15,000–20,000 BV BV60%. This supports the described pattern of earlier breakthrough in Well 4.

claim_assessments.claim_text: For colloidal AC in simulated groundwater, DOM of different MW distributions decreases adsorption for all PFAA, more strongly for short‑chain species; high DOM scenarios substantially shorten modeled breakthrough times and barrier longevity for PFBA/PFBS relative to PFOA/PFOS [S14].
claim_assessments.rationale: S14-E01 describes DOM decreasing adsorption of all PFAA in a chain‑length dependent manner, with short‑chain more impacted; S14-E03 and E05 emphasize DOM with different MW distributions and note that modeled CAC barrier longevity is particularly limited for short‑chain PFAA. This is consistent with the stated effect on breakthrough times and relative longevity.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In raw landfill leachate with high DOM, modified CFA can still remove 88% TOC and 93% UV254 at 400 g/L [S11], but PFAS capacities are modest (3.5 mg/g in pure solutions; tens of ng/g for aggregated groups in leachate) [S11].
claim_assessments.rationale: S11-E03 reports that modified CFA achieved up to 88% TOC removal and 93% UV254 decrease at 400 g/L in landfill leachate. S11-E03 and E05 state CFA PFAS adsorption capacity in pure PFAS solutions reached 3.5 mg/g (3–15% of AC capacity) and S11-E08 quantifies short- and long‑chain PFAS adsorbed from leachate as 39–60 and 4.7–9.4 ng/g respectively. This supports the contrast between strong DOM removal and modest PFAS capacities.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In IX systems, sulfate and nitrate compete for exchange sites; median PFAS–vs–chloride selectivity is high (K_PFAS/Cl ≈595), but median sulfate/chloride selectivity is lower (~189), and since sulfate concentrations often exceed nitrate, sulfate is highlighted as a practical interferent [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-R02 gives median K_PFAS/Cl = 595.3 and median K_SO4/Cl = 188.9. S01-E07 notes that PFAS have highest selectivity vs chloride, then sulfate and nitrate, and states that because sulfate concentrations in drinking water are typically higher than nitrate, sulfate is a more significant interfering ion. This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In CAC systems, increased ionic strength (NaCl) preferentially suppresses adsorption of short‑chain PFAA, due to competitive anion adsorption and reduction of electrostatic contributions; long‑chain PFAA are less affected because hydrophobic interactions dominate [S14].
claim_assessments.rationale: S14-E01 reports that inorganic anions decreased adsorption for short‑chain PFAA more than long‑chain PFAA; S14-E08 discusses ionic strength and DOM impacts and notes that DOM and polymers can behave similarly via electrostatic effects, with dual hydrophobic/electrostatic interactions (S14-E06). However, explicit data for NaCl specifically and the mechanistic partitioning (competitive anion adsorption vs reduced electrostatics vs hydrophobic dominance) are inferred rather than fully spelled out, so the detailed mechanistic explanation is only partially supported.

claim_assessments.claim_text: For modified CFA, cations (Na⁺, Ca²⁺) and anions (Cl⁻, CO₃²⁻) can promote PFAS adsorption via cation‑bridging and ligand exchange on metal‑oxide surfaces, but these effects are secondary to hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions [S11].
claim_assessments.rationale: S11-E07 explains that Na+ and Ca2+ can increase PFAS adsorption on mineral adsorbents via cation bridging, and that anions like Cl– and CO3²– can enhance PFOS adsorption via ligand exchange on metal oxide surfaces. S11-E03/E05 highlight that overall mechanisms are dominated by chemisorption, monolayer adsorption, and hydrophobic/electrostatic interactions, while H‑bonding, cation‑bridging, and metal‑oxide complexation “played minor roles.” This supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In IX, PFOA/PFOS removal and DOC co‑removal at pH 7 with 5 mg C/L NOM are robust; film diffusion—not equilibrium capacity—limits uptake at ≤50 µg/L when resin dose is low (100 mg/L) [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E03/E08 describe equilibrium and kinetic studies at pH ~7 with 5 mg C/L NOM and show EBC modeling fits; S06-E07 notes that film diffusion is the limiting factor for PFOA and PFOS at C0 ≤50 µg/L and resin dose 100 mg/L. S06-E04 reports complete PFAS removal with >60% DOC removal under some conditions. Thus the statements about robust removal, DOC co‑removal, and film‑diffusion limitation are supported; however the term “robust” is interpretive and not directly used, so this is slightly extrapolative but still largely grounded.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In RSSCTs with artificial groundwaters, higher pH generally increased sorption across all PFAS and sorbents, yielding slower breakthrough and higher modeled q₀ in Thomas fits [S15].
claim_assessments.rationale: S15-E06 states that higher pH generally increased sorption across all PFAS and sorbents, resulting in slower breakthrough and higher calculated q0 values from Thomas modeling. This directly supports the claim’s qualitative description.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In AER columns, desorption of PFBA and PFPeA occurs at later BVs (e.g., PFBA/PFPeA effluent exceeding influent at ~30,000 and ~70,000 BVs in a commercial AER, and ~60,000 and ~150,000 BVs in Gel(12‑1‑1)), attributed to displacement by long‑chain PFAS or stronger sorbates [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E03 describes column tests where PFBA and PFPeA effluent concentrations exceeded influent around 30,000 and 70,000 BV in PFA694E and 60,000 and 150,000 BV in Gel(12‑1‑1), explaining this as due to weak interactions and displacement by long‑chain PFAS or coexisting substances with stronger affinity. This matches both the numeric and mechanistic parts of the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Similar displacement patterns are seen for PFBA/PFBS on CAC in binary systems: PFOS and PFOA reduce PFBA removal by up to 56% and PFBS removal by 30.2% relative to single‑solute cases [S07].
claim_assessments.rationale: S07-E02 and S07-E05 report competitive adsorption in binary systems and note that the highest reduction in PFBA removal was –56% with PFOA, and that PFOS reduced PFBA and PFBS removal by –13.7% and –30.2% respectively. This supports the described magnitude and pattern of displacement.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Many batch studies operate at mg/L levels for capacity and kinetics (e.g., 10 mg/L PFAS for AC/biochar [S13]; 0.4 mg/L per PFCA on CFA [S11]; 0.1–1 mg/L on CAC BM [S07]).
claim_assessments.rationale: S13-E02 and E08 indicate initial concentrations of 10 mg/L for PFOA, PFOS, GenX and Cd(II) in batch tests; S11-E02 notes 0.4 mg/L each of five PFAS in DI water, and S11-E05 mentions isotherm initial concentrations 0.5–2.5 mg/L; S07-E03 describes batch tests with initial PFAS concentration range 0.1–1.0 mg/L. These values align with the cited examples.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Where more realistic ng/L influents are used (e.g., 5 ng/L per PFAS in tap water on GAC [S12], 4 ng/L regulatory limit columns on AERs [S01]), removal of most PFAS is modest on GAC (<50%) at practical GAC doses [S12], whereas a highly selective gel AER maintains PFOS/PFOA and several other PFAS below 10 ng/L up to 180,000 BVs and meets 4 ng/L PFOS/PFOA limits up to ~97,000 BVs [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S12-E05 and E01 describe tap water spiked with 5 ng/L per PFAS and report PFAS removal below 50% for most compounds with the tested GAC doses. S01-E01 reports that in RSSCTs with drinking water, Gel(12‑1‑1) maintained PFBS, PFHxS, PFOS, PFOA, PFNA, and GenX below 10 ng/L during 180,000 BVs and that it could treat 97,000 BV before PFOS/PFOA reached 4 ng/L, whereas PFA694E reached 4 ng/L at 42,000 BV. This supports the contrasted performance.
